author: John Brooke
title: System Usability Scale (SUS)
statement: 10-item questionnaire with 5-point agreement scale; alternating positive and negative items. Items: 1. I think that I would like to use this system frequently. | 2. I found the system unnecessarily complex. | 3. I thought the system was easy to use. | 4. I think that I would need the support of a technical person to be able to use this system. | 5. I found the various functions in this system were well integrated. | 6. I thought there was too much inconsistency in this system. | 7. I would imagine that most people would learn to use this system very quickly. | 8. I found the system very cumbersome to use. | 9. I felt very confident using the system. | 10. I needed to learn a lot of things before I could get going with this system.
rationale: Score: odd items (score − 1), even items (5 − score); sum × 2.5 → 0–100. Not a percentage. Reliable with small samples (~12+ for stable estimates).
threshold: Average ≈ 68 (50th percentile). Sauro–Lewis curved grade: A+ ≥ 84.1, A ≥ 80.8, B ≈ 74–77, C ≈ 65–71, D 51.7–62.6, F < 51.7. Bangor adjective scale: ~71 "good", ~85 "excellent".
citation: Brooke, J. (1996). SUS: A quick and dirty usability scale. In Jordan et al. (Eds.), Usability Evaluation in Industry, 189–194; Bangor, A., Kortum, P., & Miller, J. (2009). Determining what individual SUS scores mean. JUS, 4(3), 114–123; Sauro, J. & Lewis, J. R. (2016). Quantifying the User Experience, 2nd ed.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Kraig Finstad
title: Usability Metric for User Experience (UMUX)
statement: 4-item questionnaire aligned with ISO 9241-11: "This system’s capabilities meet my requirements." "Using this system is a frustrating experience." "This system is easy to use." "I have to spend too much time correcting things with this system." (7-point scale)
rationale: Score transformed to 0–100, correlates highly with SUS.
citation: Finstad, K. (2010). The usability metric for user experience. Interacting with Computers, 22(5), 323–327.

source_org: James R. Lewis, Brian Utesch & Deborah Maher
author: James R. Lewis, Brian Utesch & Deborah Maher
title: UMUX-LITE

rationale: Regression-adjusted score approximates SUS.
citation: Lewis, J. R., Utesch, B. S., & Maher, D. E. (2013). UMUX-LITE: When there's no time for the SUS. CHI '13, 2099–2102.

author: James R. Lewis
title: Post-Study System Usability Questionnaire (PSSUQ) / CSUQ

author: John Chin, Virginia Diehl & Kent Norman

author: Sandra Hart & Lowell Staveland
title: NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX)

author: Fred Reichheld
title: Net Promoter Score (NPS)

author: Industry practice
title: Customer Satisfaction (CSAT)

source_org: Matthew Dixon, Karen Freeman & Nicholas Toman
author: Matthew Dixon, Karen Freeman & Nicholas Toman
title: Customer Effort Score (CES)

source_org: Kerry Rodden, Hilary Hutchinson & Xin Fu (Google)
author: Kerry Rodden, Hilary Hutchinson & Xin Fu (Google)
title: HEART framework

author: Usability practice
title: Task success (completion) rate
statement: Percentage of participants who complete a task correctly (binary or with partial credit).

citation: Sauro, J. (2011). What is a good task-completion rate? MeasuringU; Sauro & Lewis (2016).

author: Usability practice
title: Time on task
statement: Time to complete a task, typically for successful attempts only.

author: Usability practice
title: Error rate
statement: Number or proportion of errors per task or opportunities for error.
rationale: Classify errors by severity and type (slip vs. mistake).

author: Jeff Sauro & Erika Kindlund
title: Single Usability Metric (SUM)
statement: Combines completion, time, errors and satisfaction into one standardized score.

author: Pauline Smith
title: Lostness measure
statement: L = √[(N/S − 1)² + (R/N − 1)²], where N = distinct pages visited, S = total pages visited, R = minimum pages required.
rationale: Compute from navigation logs per task.
citation: Smith, P. A. (1996). Towards a practical measure of hypertext usability. Interacting with Computers, 8(4), 365–381.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Bob Bailey & Cari Wolfson
title: First-click success
statement: Whether the first click on a task is correct.
rationale: First-click testing on designs or live pages.
threshold: Correct first click → ~87% task success vs ~46% when the first click is wrong.
citation: Bailey, R. W., Wolfson, C. A., Nall, J., & Koyani, S. (2009). Performance-based usability testing: Metrics that have the greatest impact for improving a system's usability. HCD 2009, LNCS 5619, 3–12.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Jakob Nielsen
title: Usability problem severity rating
statement: 0 = not a problem; 1 = cosmetic; 2 = minor; 3 = major (important to fix, high priority); 4 = usability catastrophe (imperative to fix before release). Severity combines frequency, impact and persistence (plus market impact).
rationale: Have multiple evaluators rate independently and average.
citation: Nielsen, J. (1995). Severity Ratings for Usability Problems. NN/g.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Intercom (Sean McBride)
title: RICE prioritization
statement: Score = Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort.
rationale: Use to prioritize audit fixes against product work.
citation: McBride, S. (2016). RICE: Simple prioritization for product managers. Intercom blog.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Noriaki Kano et al.
title: Kano model
statement: Classifies features as must-be (basic), one-dimensional (performance), attractive (delighters), indifferent or reverse, based on functional/dysfunctional question pairs.
rationale: Survey users with paired questions.
citation: Kano, N., Seraku, N., Takahashi, F., & Tsuji, S. (1984). Attractive quality and must-be quality. Journal of the Japanese Society for Quality Control, 14(2), 39–48.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Rudolf Flesch
title: Flesch Reading Ease
statement: RE = 206.835 − 1.015 × (words/sentences) − 84.6 × (syllables/words).
rationale: Compute on body copy.
threshold: 60–70 = plain English; ≥ 60 recommended for general audiences.
citation: Flesch, R. (1948). A new readability yardstick. Journal of Applied Psychology, 32(3), 221–233.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: J. Peter Kincaid et al.
title: Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level
statement: FKGL = 0.39 × (words/sentences) + 11.8 × (syllables/words) − 15.59.
rationale: Compute on body copy.
threshold: Aim for grade 8 or lower for general public content (US); WCAG 3.1.5 lower secondary.
citation: Kincaid, J. P., Fishburne, R. P., Rogers, R. L., & Chissom, B. S. (1975). Derivation of new readability formulas for Navy enlisted personnel. Research Branch Report 8-75.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Robert Gunning
title: Gunning Fog Index
statement: Fog = 0.4 × [(words/sentences) + 100 × (complex words/words)], complex = 3+ syllables.
citation: Gunning, R. (1952). The Technique of Clear Writing. McGraw-Hill.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: G. Harry McLaughlin
title: SMOG grade
statement: SMOG = 1.0430 × √(polysyllables × 30/sentences) + 3.1291.
rationale: Common in health communication.
citation: McLaughlin, G. H. (1969). SMOG grading: A new readability formula. Journal of Reading, 12(8), 639–646.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Meri Coleman & T. L. Liau
title: Coleman–Liau index
statement: CLI = 0.0588 × L − 0.296 × S − 15.8 (L = letters per 100 words, S = sentences per 100 words).
rationale: Character-based; easy to compute.
citation: Coleman, M. & Liau, T. L. (1975). A computer readability formula designed for machine scoring. Journal of Applied Psychology, 60(2), 283–284.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: E. A. Smith & R. J. Senter
author: E. A. Smith & R. J. Senter
title: Automated Readability Index (ARI)
statement: ARI = 4.71 × (characters/words) + 0.5 × (words/sentences) − 21.43.
citation: Smith, E. A. & Senter, R. J. (1967). Automated readability index. AMRL-TR-66-220.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Edgar Dale & Jeanne Chall
title: Dale–Chall readability formula
statement: Uses a list of ~3,000 familiar words; score = 0.1579 × (% difficult words) + 0.0496 × (words/sentences), +3.6365 if difficult words > 5%.
citation: Dale, E. & Chall, J. S. (1948). A formula for predicting readability. Educational Research Bulletin, 27(1), 11–28.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: W3C
title: Color contrast ratio (WCAG)
statement: Contrast = (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05), where L is relative luminance computed from linearized sRGB (0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B).
rationale: Compute for text/background and UI component pairs.
threshold: Text ≥ 4.5:1 (AA), large text ≥ 3:1 (AA), ≥ 7:1 (AAA); non-text UI and graphics ≥ 3:1.
citation: W3C (2008/2023). WCAG 2 relative luminance and contrast ratio definitions.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Andrew Somers (Myndex)
title: APCA (Accessible Perceptual Contrast Algorithm)
statement: Perceptually based lightness contrast (Lc) that accounts for polarity and font weight/size; candidate for WCAG 3 (not normative).
threshold: Lc 75 for body text, Lc 90 preferred; Lc 60 for large/bold text (guideline values).
citation: Somers, A. APCA Readability Criterion (draft). Myndex Research.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: ISO; I. S. MacKenzie
title: Fitts throughput (ISO 9241-9 / 9241-411)
statement: Throughput (bits/s) = effective index of difficulty ÷ movement time, used to compare pointing devices.
citation: ISO 9241-411:2012. Evaluation methods for the design of physical input devices.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Google
title: Core Web Vitals
statement: LCP (loading), INP (interactivity; replaced FID in March 2024), CLS (visual stability), assessed at the 75th percentile.
rationale: Field data (CrUX) and lab tools (Lighthouse).
citation: Google web.dev (2020–2024). Web Vitals.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Analytics practice
title: Conversion rate & funnel drop-off
statement: Share of users completing a goal; funnel analysis shows step-level abandonment.
rationale: Combine with qualitative research to find why users drop.
threshold: Average documented online cart abandonment ≈ 70% (Baymard Institute meta-analysis).
citation: Baymard Institute. Cart Abandonment Rate statistics (meta-analysis of ~50 studies).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Product analytics practice
title: Retention & churn

rationale: Cohort analysis.
citation: Industry practice.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Jakob Nielsen & Rolf Molich
title: Heuristic evaluation
statement: Experts independently inspect an interface against a set of usability heuristics, then aggregate and rate findings by severity.
rationale: Fast, cheap inspection at any stage; complements but does not replace user testing.
citation: Nielsen & Molich (1990). CHI '90.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: Clayton Lewis, Peter Polson, Cathleen Wharton & John Rieman
author: Clayton Lewis, Peter Polson, Cathleen Wharton & John Rieman
title: Cognitive walkthrough
statement: Evaluators step through a task asking whether a new user would know what to do and whether feedback shows progress.

author: Randolph Bias
title: Pluralistic walkthrough

source_org: Usability engineering practice (e.g., J. Dumas & J. Redish)
author: Usability engineering practice (e.g., J. Dumas & J. Redish)
title: Usability testing (moderated / unmoderated)

source_org: K. A. Ericsson & H. A. Simon; C. Lewis
author: K. A. Ericsson & H. A. Simon; C. Lewis
title: Think-aloud protocol
statement: Participants verbalize their thoughts while performing tasks (concurrent) or afterward (retrospective).

source_org: Michael Medlock, Dennis Wixon et al. (Microsoft)
author: Michael Medlock, Dennis Wixon et al. (Microsoft)

author: Online controlled experiment practice

author: Information architecture practice

author: Donna Spencer; Dave O'Brien

author: Bob Bailey & Cari Wolfson
title: First-click testing

author: Christine Perfetti; UIE

source_org: Research practice (e.g., J. Nielsen & K. Pernice 2010)
author: Research practice (e.g., J. Nielsen & K. Pernice 2010)

author: Research practice
